topics.title: Geography by numbers
topics.intro: Geographers use maths to compare places: average earnings, rainfall, population density and growth. Your maths skills do the work here.
topics.teach: Explain what population density means and how to work it out.
topics.talk: Ask her whether a village or a city has a higher population density, and why.

items.prompt: The mean of these earnings is £800 but the median is £450. Which average better describes a typical household?

options.text: The median: one high earner pulls the mean up
The mean, because it uses every number
options.feedback: Using every number is usually a strength, but here one household (£2,250) drags the mean far above what four of the five households earn.

options.text: Neither: you cannot average sums of money
options.feedback: You can! Geographers and governments average earnings all the time.

items.explain: When one value is far bigger than the rest, the median gives a fairer picture of a typical household. That is why average earnings in a country are usually reported as a median.
items.passage:
Weekly earnings of five households on one street:
£400   £420   £450   £480   £2,250

items.prompt: Which island is more densely populated?

options.feedback: A has more people, but they are spread over four times the area. A: 1,200 ÷ 40 = 30 people per km².
Work out people ÷ area for each one.

items.explain: Population density = people ÷ area. A: 1,200 ÷ 40 = 30 per km². B: 900 ÷ 10 = 90 per km², three times as crowded.
items.passage:
Island A: 1,200 people, area 40 km²
Island B: 900 people, area 10 km²

items.prompt: What pattern does this rainfall data show?

options.text: Wet winters and very dry summers
Rain spread evenly through the year
options.feedback: Look at the numbers: 120 mm in December but only 2 mm in July.
Check which months are which: the big numbers are November to February.

items.explain: This pattern is typical of a Mediterranean climate, like southern Spain or Greece: hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters.
items.passage:
Rainfall (mm) in a coastal town
Jan 110 · Feb 95 · Mar 70 · Apr 40 · May 20 · Jun 5
Jul 2 · Aug 5 · Sep 25 · Oct 70 · Nov 100 · Dec 120

items.prompt: Which reading is most likely a mistake?

options.feedback: The highest value isn’t automatically wrong: 24°C is normal for July.

options.text: None: all weather data is correct
options.feedback: Instruments and people make mistakes. Results that don’t fit the pattern should be checked.

items.explain: 4°C at midday in a UK July is almost impossible. Like an anomaly in a science experiment, it should be checked, and left out of the mean if it was a mistake.
items.passage:
Midday temperature (°C) in a UK town, one week in July
Mon 21 · Tue 23 · Wed 22 · Thu 4 · Fri 24 · Sat 22 · Sun 23

items.prompt: In a survey of 200 people in a town, 50 travel to work by bus. What percentage is that?
In a country, 4 out of every 5 people live in towns and cities. What fraction live in the countryside?
items.explain: The fractions must add up to one whole: 1 − 4/5 = 1/5. The UK is a bit more urban than this: over 80% of people live in towns and cities.
